issues.legal_issue: Property that has automatically vested in a custodian under provincial evacuee-property law and is carried forward under successor central legislation does not require a fresh declaration under the central legislation.
material_facts: A partner left for Pakistan amid disturbed conditions and was held to be an evacuee under provincial law.
The evacuee’s interest in the partnership business, including its property in the province, vested automatically in the Custodian under that law.
The successor central ordinance and Act provided that property already vested would be deemed to continue vested.
The firm contended that a fresh notice and declaration under the central law were necessary.
issues.conclusion: No fresh notice or declaration under section 7 was necessary because the interest had already vested automatically and continued to vest under the successor legislation.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 2(c), 2(d) and 5 of the U.P. Administration of Evacuee Property Ordinance, 1949, an evacuee’s property interest in the province vested automatically in the Custodian. Sections 8(2) and 55(3) of the Central Administration of Evacuee Property Ordinance, 1949, and sections 8(2) and 58(3) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, continued that vesting by deeming provisions and savings clauses. Section 7 applied to property not already vested automatically; it did not require a further declaration for property whose vesting had already continued under the successor legislation. The Court also referred to the retrospective validation considered in Azimunnissa v. The Deputy Custodian, Evacuee Properties, District Deoria, [1961] 2 S.C.R. 91.

predicates.successor_regime_proceeding: The dispute concerns property under a successor regime that carries forward property previously vested under an earlier evacuee-property regime.
predicates.property_previously_vested: The property interest had already vested automatically in a custodian under the earlier regime.
predicates.departure_triggered_evacuee_status: A person left the relevant territory for another country because of disturbed conditions and was treated as an evacuee under the applicable law.

issues.definition: When a successor-regime proceeding concerns property already vested because a person’s departure triggered evacuee status, no fresh declaration is required.

issues.legal_issue: Partners cannot claim a fundamental right in an evacuee partner’s interest that has vested in the Custodian and has been declared evacuee property by a final, unchallenged order.
material_facts: The evacuee partner’s interest in the firm had vested in the Custodian.
An order declared that interest to be evacuee property, and the firm did not appeal or otherwise challenge that order under the Act.
The firm and its partners later claimed that orders concerning the evacuee’s interest infringed their fundamental rights.
issues.conclusion: The partners had no fundamental right in respect of the evacuee’s interest in the partnership, which had vested in the Custodian and been declared evacuee property by an unchallenged final order.
issues.legal_principle: Because the evacuee’s interest had vested in the Custodian, the other partners had no interest in that share. The prior order declaring it evacuee property had become final when it was not challenged through the available process, and could no longer be questioned in the later proceedings. The Court therefore held that the partners had no fundamental right in respect of that interest. The remaining claims concerning the partners’ own rights were not finally resolved in the Article 32 petition; that petition was dismissed without prejudice while the related appeals were remanded for consideration of the other issues.

predicates.fundamental_rights_proceeding: A party seeks constitutional relief on the ground that action concerning an evacuee’s property interest infringes fundamental rights.
predicates.evacuee_interest_vested: The evacuee’s interest in the property has vested in a custodian, leaving the other partners without an interest in that share.
predicates.prior_property_order_final: An order declaring the interest to be evacuee property was not challenged through the available process and became final.

issues.definition: In a fundamental-rights proceeding, where the evacuee’s interest has vested and the declaration of evacuee property is final, the other partners have no fundamental right in that vested interest.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court has territorial jurisdiction to issue an appropriate writ against a state-appointed appellate officer who functions under state law within the state, even if the officer’s head office is located outside the state for administrative convenience.
material_facts: The Appellate Officer was appointed by the State Government under the Evacuee Interest (Separation) Act, with jurisdiction over specified local areas.
The officer heard and decided the appeal in the state and functioned there under the state statute.
The officer’s head office and records were later located in Delhi for convenience, and the same officer also served other states.
The High Court dismissed the writ petitions on the ground that the appellate order had merged with an order made by an authority located outside its territory.
issues.conclusion: The Allahabad High Court had jurisdiction under Article 226 to issue an appropriate writ against the Appellate Officer, notwithstanding the location of the officer’s head office in Delhi.
issues.legal_principle: Article 226, as it stood before amendment, generally required the person or authority to reside or be located within the High Court’s territorial jurisdiction. The Court distinguished Election Commission, India v. Saka Venkata Subba Rao, [1953] S.C.R. 1144; Lt. Col. Khajoor Singh v. Union of India, [1961] 2 S.C.R. 828; A. Thangal Kunju Musaliar v. V. Venkitachalam Potti, [1955] 2 S.C.R. 1196; Collector of Customs v. East India Commercial Company, [1963] 2 S.C.R. 563; Shriram Jhunjhunwala v. State of Bombay, A.I.R. 1962 S.C. 670; and State of Uttar Pradesh v. Mohammad Nooh, [1958] S.C.R. 595. Those cases did not concern an appellate authority appointed by the State Government that legally and factually functioned within the state under state law. Such an authority is located within the High Court’s territorial limits for deciding appeals under that law, even if its head office is elsewhere for convenience.

rule.if: territorial_writ_proceeding and state_appointed_appellate_authority and state_law_local_function and outside_head_office_only_for_convenience

predicates.territorial_writ_proceeding: A party seeks a writ from a High Court against an appellate authority whose head office is outside that High Court’s territory.
predicates.state_appointed_appellate_authority: The appellate authority was appointed by the State Government under a state law.
predicates.state_law_local_function: The authority exercises its statutory appellate function for local areas in the state and hears or decides the relevant appeal there.
predicates.outside_head_office_only_for_convenience: The authority’s head office is outside the state for administrative convenience, rather than because its relevant statutory function is located there.

issues.definition: A High Court has territorial writ jurisdiction when a state-appointed appellate authority performs its local statutory function within the state and has an outside head office only for convenience.
